concepts.name: Fallback policy for endpoints without authorization metadata
SameSite=None and Secure for cross-site cookies

questions.prompt: An ASP.NET Core team wants endpoints without explicit authorization metadata to require an authenticated user by default. Which configuration serves that purpose?

choices.text: Set the CORS policy to require credentials for every origin
Configure FallbackPolicy to require an authenticated user
Set a cookie expiration date without an authorization policy
Register a role handler but omit every endpoint policy

questions.explanation: FallbackPolicy covers requests without explicit authorization metadata. Authentication, role-handler registration, and CORS alone do not impose that default authorization requirement.

sources.title: Create an app with data protected by authorization
sources.claim: A fallback policy can require authentication on endpoints without authorization metadata; AllowAnonymous bypasses authorization.

questions.prompt: An authentication flow needs a cookie on a cross-site POST callback. Under the modern SameSite standard, which cookie attributes permit that use?

choices.text: SameSite=None and Secure on the cookie
SameSite=Strict with Secure removed for the callback
SameSite=Lax with HttpOnly removed for the callback
SameSite=None without Secure to support HTTP callbacks

questions.explanation: None permits cross-site use and requires Secure. Strict and Lax can block cross-site POST cookies; HttpOnly addresses script access, not this SameSite restriction.

sources.title: Work with SameSite cookies in ASP.NET Core
sources.claim: SameSite=None permits cross-site cookie use and requires Secure under the 2019 standard; Strict or Lax can disrupt cross-site POST authentication flows.

questions.prompt: Cookie authentication enables sliding expiration with a 20-minute expiration window. Which behaviors match that option? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The option renews cookies in browsers without incoming requests
A request early in the window need not cause sliding renewal
Every request renews the cookie from the very first minute
A request after the window's midpoint can reissue the cookie
A renewed cookie receives a new expiration time

questions.explanation: Sliding renewal is request-driven and occurs after more than half the window has elapsed. It reissues the cookie with a new expiration; it is not renewal on every request or a background browser timer.

sources.title: CookieAuthenticationOptions.SlidingExpiration
sources.claim: Sliding expiration reissues the cookie with a new expiration when a request is processed more than halfway through its expiration window.

questions.prompt: A fallback policy requires authentication globally. A login endpoint is explicitly marked AllowAnonymous. What does that marker do?

choices.text: It overrides the bypass when the caller has an expired cookie
It asks the fallback policy to enforce the default user role
It bypasses authorization for this endpoint
It requires both the fallback policy and a named login policy

questions.explanation: AllowAnonymous permits the endpoint without authorization even when a fallback policy is configured. Otherwise a global authenticated-user requirement could block the login route itself.

sources.title: Create an app with data protected by authorization
sources.claim: A fallback policy can require authentication on endpoints without authorization metadata; AllowAnonymous bypasses authorization.

questions.prompt: A team changes every authentication cookie to SameSite=Strict. Why can a third-party login flow using a cross-site POST callback break?

choices.text: Strict requires JavaScript to manually append the cookie header
Strict causes the browser to delete the cookie before each redirect
Strict makes the cookie valid only for cross-origin API requests
Strict can prevent the cookie from accompanying the callback

questions.explanation: SameSite restricts cross-site transmission. The callback may need a cookie that Strict withholds; this is distinct from cookie deletion or a JavaScript header mechanism.

sources.title: Work with SameSite cookies in ASP.NET Core
sources.claim: SameSite=None permits cross-site cookie use and requires Secure under the 2019 standard; Strict or Lax can disrupt cross-site POST authentication flows.

questions.prompt: An ASP.NET Core app relies on sliding cookie expiration. Which claims are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A new expiration can be issued after the midpoint is passed
Sliding renewal always happens immediately after sign-in
The option periodically contacts browsers while they are idle
Early requests always extend the expiration window immediately
Renewal is evaluated when the app processes a request

questions.explanation: Requests processed beyond the midpoint can trigger reissuance and a new expiration. The option does not independently contact idle browsers and does not require extension for early requests.

sources.title: CookieAuthenticationOptions.SlidingExpiration
sources.claim: Sliding expiration reissues the cookie with a new expiration when a request is processed more than halfway through its expiration window.
